title: Treatment hierarchies across target populations
question: Does a treatment hierarchy move more across plausible target populations than across sampling variability, so that a hierarchy must name its population?
design: Star networks of five treatments against a reference with treatment-specific linear modification; fixed-effect meta-regression and P-scores at three targets; rank movement across targets against movement across independent replicates. 24 cells, 1000 replicates each.
answer: Yes: where effect modification changed the true ranking across plausible targets, the estimated hierarchy moved 1.6 to 2.4 places per treatment across targets against 0.1 to 1.4 places across sampling replicates, so a hierarchy must name its population. But estimated hierarchies also moved 0.2 to 2.1 places across targets where the true ranking did not change, through the uncertainty of meta-regression slopes away from the data's center, so a changed hierarchy is not by itself evidence of population dependence.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: in all 10 scenarios with a true rank change, movement across targets exceeded movement across replicates beyond Monte Carlo error.
Spurious movement across targets with no true change: 0.23 to 2.07 places per treatment.
Best treatment misidentified at an outer target in up to 70% of analyses (two trials per comparison, closely spaced effects).
not_answered: Study-level meta-regression rather than ML-NMR; P-scores only; one covariate; fixed-effect. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Treatment ranks (P-scores) at declared target covariate means
methods_compared: fixed-effect meta-regression with P-scores at each target
